extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors and small businesses with limited resources seeking pro bono attorney representation to file a patent
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on eligibility requirements and the application process for the USPTO Nationwide Patent Pro Bono Program — who qualifies for free attorney representation and how to apply. Covers income limits, demonstration of patent-system knowledge, invention documentation, regional variations, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — three basic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, there are three basic requirements: maximum household income; knowledge of the patent system; and you must have an invention - not just an idea!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the high-level eligibility test used by regional pro bono programs; details and thresholds vary by region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum household income
rubrics_metrics.description: You must earn less than the regional program's income limitation. Region dependent, but usually 300% of federal poverty levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check your regional program's web site to determine your income limitation. Example given: a single person could have an income of up to $45,180 (3 times the current single person poverty level of $15,060).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the patent system (demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways to demonstrate your knowledge of the patent system: Have a current provisional or nonprovisional patent application on file with the USPTO OR Successfully complete the on-line certificate training course (certificado de formación en español).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NOTE: Some regional programs require that a provisional patent application be filed as a condition of requesting assistance. NOTE: Many regional pro bono programs require successful completion of the certificate training to be considered for the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must have an invention — not just an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you can obtain a pro bono attorney, you will have to have an actual invention, not merely an idea. To demonstrate an invention, you should be able to describe the invention so that someone else could actually make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAUTION: Do not publicly disclose your invention prior to filing a patent application or at least a provisional application for a patent. Public disclosure could create prior art and prevent obtaining a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to apply for pro bono assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: You can apply for pro bono assistance to file a patent application for your invention by contacting the regional Patent Pro Bono Program in the state where you live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access your regional program’s website via the regional program map and contact the regional program. Email probono@uspto.gov if you have questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional program variation and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility requirements vary for each regional program and some impose additional conditions (for example, requiring a provisional application or certificate training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must check their specific regional program website for exact income limits, required paperwork, and any additional prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available training and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The program provides a series of short videos and a webinar; applicants are referred to additional resources such as the Inventors and Entrepreneurs Resources page, Patent and Trademark Resource Centers (PTRCs), IP Awareness Assessment Tool, and Process for Obtaining a Utility Patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many regional programs require completion of the USPTO certificate training course; watch the training videos and webinar to learn more and prepare application materials. Other resources include a patent pro bono inventor flyer and training video links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program authority and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pro Bono Program stems from the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA) and an Executive Action directing the USPTO to expand pro bono coverage to all 50 states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background information on the statutory/administrative basis for the program; indicates nationwide coverage intent but implementation is via regional programs.
